title: A meal everyone can eat
hookLine: langar food is kept vegetarian so that anyone can share it

cards: Planning a party for a mixed group of friends is a puzzle. One doesn't eat pork. One eats only halal.
One is vegetarian, one is vegan, one has a nut allergy, one just really hates mushrooms. You end up texting everyone, checking labels, making three versions of the same dish.
Now multiply that by thousands of guests you've never met, from every religion and none, walking in off the street all day, every day, and nobody fills in a form.
How do you feed them all without anyone having to ask what's in the pot? The langar's answer is simple, and it's an old one.

teach.b: Langar is kept vegetarian. Dal, a pot of lentils. A vegetable dish.
Rice, rotis, maybe yogurt, maybe kheer, a sweet rice pudding.
Simple food, and nothing on the plate that would stop a guest from eating it. Think about who could walk in. Hindus who don't eat beef.
Muslims and Jews who don't eat pork. Jains and some Hindus who eat no meat at all. Sikhs whose own practice keeps them vegetarian.
Visitors with no religious rule who just want to be sure. With a vegetarian langar, none of them has to ask. The meal says welcome before anyone opens their mouth.
That's the key idea: the food is shaped by the guests, not the cooks. The goal isn't a rule about what people should eat. It's making sure no one is left out of the row.
Honestly, Sikhs themselves differ about meat in their own homes. Some are strictly vegetarian; others eat meat, and Sikh codes of conduct forbid meat that has been ritually slaughtered.
In the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase, that fools argue over flesh and meat without understanding wisdom, and Sikhs read that passage in more than one way.
But on the langar there's no argument: it's vegetarian, so everyone can eat. You don't have to be vegetarian to learn from this.
The question works at any table: when I set out food, who could eat it, and who would be left out?

how: Gurdwaras serve a simple vegetarian langar, typically dal, a vegetable dish, rice and rotis, so that people of any faith or diet can eat it; Sikhs themselves hold differing views about eating meat at home.

o: a pot of lentils, the heart of langar
a spiced rice dish served on feast days
a yogurt drink served with the meal

games.q: what's inside the meal — tap the pairs.

s: langar is vegetarian because all Sikhs are vegetarian
Sikhs differ at home. langar is kept vegetarian so that anyone can eat it.
Sikh codes of conduct forbid ritually slaughtered meat
that's one point on which Sikh practice about meat is clear.
the point of a vegetarian langar is to tell guests what to eat
the point is that no one is left out of the row.

games.q: you're cooking for thousands of strangers of every faith and none, and nobody fills in a form. how do you make sure everyone can eat?
o: cook several menus and ask each guest.
cook what the cooks like best.
games.why: langar is kept vegetarian so that no one has to ask what's in the pot. the meal says welcome first.

practice: Picture a table in your home with five chairs, filled with people you know who eat differently: one who doesn't eat meat, one who avoids pork, one with an allergy, one who's picky, one who just needs something warm.
Plan one simple meal they could all eat without anyone having to ask, lentils, rice, vegetables, bread, and picture them all reaching for the same pot.

wordCard.voice: Dal. The pot of lentils at the heart of langar, kept simple and vegetarian, so that no guest, of any faith or diet, has to ask what's in it.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: lentils, the heart of the langar plate.

carryVoice: Your line: everyone can eat this. No one has to ask what's in the pot. That's day one hundred seventeen.
